My 2 cents. I'm a Chemist at an international pharmaceutical company. This is a problem I see and is a big reason I don't work in academia.

A problem not covered in the link is caused by Non-Scientist bureaucrats at pretty much all universities. These non-scientists will tell the scientists on staff "You must publish <insert arbitrary number> of articles of original research a year or get fired." This leads to a lot of problems.

  1. It promotes taking research that only makes sense as a whole and splitting it into smaller chunks. This can cause the lack of reproducible results in the story as all the pieces necessary are not there.

  2. It promotes "quick and dirty" analysis by the authors and the reviewers just so you can get the paper out, whether the data is good or not. Those reviewers are also scientists with an arbitrary publishing quota and time reviewing is time not spent getting your own research published.

  3. It prevents scientists from doing long term studies. The kind of research that wins Nobel's can take decades to produce. To meet this quota you need short term studies that don't really help expand our knowledge of the world.

  4. Some researchers create their own journals just to meet these quotas, hence the gibberish paper getting accepted in the article.

  5. Verifying someone else's work does not count towards keeping their jobs so no one will do it unless its absolutely necessary.

From the Journal side of things, they rarely publish a paper that says "I tried this and it didn't work" or "I tried to replicate study X and got different results."

We could help fix this by taking away the quotas and having more scientists publicly funded with a condition that X% of their time should be spent either on peer review or performing replication studies. With the internet there is also no reason all studies and all raw data shouldn't be available for review. Especially if you tried something and found it to be wrong. Knowing what doesn't work is just as important as knowing what does.

Overall we do get better with time, but if we want to increase the speed at which we do, we need to change the incentives.

Stress builds up over time, and it is released relatively quickly. This is why there are long periods of calm, and then a lot of earthquakes at once. Intro level geology courses present a simplified view of this process in which a flat plate is subducting under another plate, and all of this is happening on a plane.

In the real world the plates have rough surfaces, and they are moving over the surface of a sphere. If you try to wrap a piece of square paper around a sphere you have to cut it and overlap it to get it to fit well, and even then there are still topographic highs and lows. These rough patches get caught whenever they subduct, and stress will build up until they break, or slip, and this is what an earthquake is. You actually get a stair step pattern on fault planes called chatter marks where you can see where the movement stops after each earthquake. These earthquakes will continue until enough stress is released that the plates are able to deform a little without breaking.
